content: Tinea corporis, commonly referred to as ringworm of the body, is a fungal infection of the skin. It is caused by mold-like fungi known as dermatophytes, which thrive in warm and moist environments. This condition can affect individuals of all ages but is particularly common in children. Symptoms of Tinea Corporis: The primary symptom of tinea corporis is itching. The rash typically begins as a small area of red, raised spots or pimples. Over time, the rash develops into a ring-shaped lesion with a red, raised, and scaly border, while the center appears clearer. These lesions can occur on various exposed areas of the body, such as the arms, legs, face, or other regions. Causes and Risk Factors: Tinea corporis is caused by dermatophytes, which are fungi that thrive in warm, moist conditions. Factors that increase the risk of developing this infection include: Prolonged moisture on the skin, such as from sweating. Minor injuries to the skin or nails. Poor hygiene practices. Transmission: Tinea corporis is highly contagious and can spread through direct contact with an infected person’s skin or by touching contaminated objects, such as clothing, combs, pool surfaces, or shower floors. Pets, particularly cats, can also carry and transmit the fungi. Diagnosis: A healthcare provider can often diagnose tinea corporis based on the appearance of the skin. In some cases, additional tests may be performed, such as: Microscopic examination of a skin scraping using a potassium hydroxide (KOH) preparation. Skin lesion biopsy. When to Seek Medical Attention: You should consult a healthcare provider if the ringworm does not improve with self-care measures or over-the-counter treatments. Treatment Options: To treat tinea corporis, it is essential to keep the affected skin clean and dry. Antifungal creams, which are available over the counter or by prescription, are commonly used. Treatment steps include: 1. Washing and drying the affected area thoroughly. 2. Applying the antifungal cream starting just outside the rash and moving toward the center. 3. Washing and drying your hands after application. 4. Using the cream twice daily for 7 to 10 days. It is important not to cover the rash with a bandage. Effective antifungal creams often contain active ingredients such as miconazole, clotrimazole, ketoconazole, terbinafine, or oxiconazole. Once treatment begins, children can typically return to school. To prevent the spread of the infection: Wash all towels in warm, soapy water and dry them thoroughly. Use a clean towel and washcloth each time. Clean sinks, bathtubs, and bathroom floors after use. Wear clean clothes daily and avoid sharing clothing. For severe cases, infections covering large areas, or those involving deeper skin layers (e.g., hair follicles in the beard area), oral antifungal medications may be prescribed. Antibiotics may also be necessary if a secondary bacterial infection develops. Additionally, infected pets should be treated to prevent reinfection. Prognosis: Tinea corporis typically responds well to topical antifungal treatments within four weeks. Severe or resistant cases usually improve quickly with oral antifungal medications.
